---
title: "What must be new at prediction time"
---

The earlier page on [populations and samples](../statistical-inference/populations-and-samples.qmd) required an inferential claim to specify the population represented by a sample. Predictive evaluation requires a related decision. We must say which responses were unavailable during fitting and what information is available when those responses are predicted.

[**Out-of-sample prediction**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html) predicts responses that did not contribute to fitting the model. This definition leaves an important question open. Does the held-out response come from an observed participant and item, or does it come from a participant or item absent from the training data?

## Specifying the held-out observations

Suppose an acceptability experiment crosses participants with sentences. Several data separations are possible.

| predictive question | participant during fitting | sentence during fitting |
|:--|:--|:--|
| another response from an observed participant to an observed sentence | observed | observed |
| a response to a new sentence from an observed participant | observed | absent |
| a response from a new participant to an observed sentence | absent | observed |
| a response from a new participant to a new sentence | absent | absent |

Every row concerns a response excluded from fitting. The rows nevertheless ask different scientific questions. A model can predict another response from represented participants and sentences while failing for a participant or sentence absent from the training data.

This is why the phrase *new observation* is incomplete. A new word might be a new token of an observed word type, a word type absent from fitting, or a word in a passage absent from fitting. The data split must encode the intended meaning of *new*.

## Stating what information is available

Holding out a participant does not by itself determine which information about that participant may be used. Imagine a model with a participant-specific baseline. If five calibration trials are available before the sixth response is predicted, the baseline may be estimated from those five trials. If the intended use is prediction for the participant's first trial, it may not.

Both procedures predict a response from a participant who was absent when the population-level model was fitted. They differ in the information available at prediction time. A report must state whether calibration responses were allowed.

The same issue arises with linguistic annotations. A model predicting an unseen verb's acceptability profile may use corpus counts for that verb while withholding all of its acceptability judgments. A model predicting a language's phonological inventory may use the language's family and region while withholding its segment inventory. These predictors are permissible only if the corresponding information would be available in the intended use setting.

## Matching the split to the question

Suppose reading times are observed from readers $s$, word positions $w$, and passages $p$. A random row split can leave one reading-time response out while retaining other responses from the same reader and passage. This evaluates another response from the represented collection of readers and passages.

A new-reader question instead requires every response from one reader to be held out together. A new-passage question requires every word position from one passage to be held out together. The [grouped cross-validation page](grouped-cross-validation.qmd) develops these separations.

The held-out group also determines the replication relevant to the claim. Fifty-five passages provide 55 opportunities to examine prediction for an omitted passage. They do not provide thousands of independent omitted passages merely because the passages contain thousands of word positions.

## Theory determines what should be held out

The data separation should follow the theoretical contrast. Suppose one account claims that comprehenders preactivate full lexical forms, while another claims that context supplies graded syntactic and semantic information. Holding out word positions within observed passages asks whether those predictors help with other positions in the same collection of texts. Holding out complete passages asks whether the fitted relation generalizes to passages absent during fitting.

The second question may be scientifically preferable when the claim concerns connected texts. It also requires passage-level replication. The choice should be made from the claim and design, not from whichever split later produces the most favorable score.

## Writing the predictive question in plain language

A complete statement answers four questions.

1. What response is predicted?
2. Which observations or groups are excluded from fitting?
3. What predictors are available for the held-out observations?
4. To which population or use setting should the result generalize?

For instance:

> The model predicts the mean log first-fixation duration of each content-word position in a passage omitted during fitting. Word length, word class, and independently collected predictability norms are available. No reading-time response from the held-out passage is used to fit the model. The score concerns omitted passages from the corpus, conditional on fixation and on the observed reader sample.

This statement is narrower than “predict natural reading.” It identifies the response, the held-out group, the permitted predictors, and the scope of the result.

## More than one predictive question may be useful

A study may evaluate more than one data separation. For instance, it may report predictions for new responses from observed readers and predictions for readers absent during fitting. Each result needs its own split and interpretation.

The results should not be pooled into one score. They estimate performance under different information conditions. A secondary analysis should also not replace the analysis that motivated the study after the results are known.

The number of groups matters. A corpus with ten stories can use each story as a held-out group, but the resulting ten story-level scores may be unstable. Showing those scores makes the available replication visible.

## Matching the question and the split

1. State the required data separation for predicting another response from an observed participant and item.
2. State the required data separation for predicting an observed item for a participant absent during fitting.
3. A lexical model estimates a word-specific baseline using all corpus occurrences, then reports prediction for word types omitted during model fitting. What information leaked into the fitted procedure?
4. Why do 100,000 word observations from ten stories not provide 100,000 independent opportunities to evaluate prediction for an omitted story?

Out-of-sample prediction requires a response excluded from fitting. A complete predictive question also states which groups are held out, which predictors remain available, and where the result should generalize. The [next page](predictive-loss.qmd) defines the numerical consequence assigned to each prediction error.
